subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RELAXATION OF IMPORT CONTROLS

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RELAXATION OF IMPORT CONTROLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house that we have just been advised of new measures of relaxation on imports into Australia from Canada and other dollar countries and as a result, effective yesterday, imports into Australia from Canada of most capital equipment, electrical machine apparatus and appliances are now given equal access to the Australian market in competition with all other suppliers under the Australian import controls. Canadian exports of these products to Australia have been faced with discriminatory restrictions. With the removal of the discrimination in this field we are hopeful that Canadian exporters will be able to increase their shipments to Australia.
Total Canadian exports of the type of products affected amounted to some $40 million last year, of which about $1 million went to Australia. In addition, a number of items have been completely removed from import controls in Australia, including magnesium.
These new measures by Australia are a welcome move in the direction of improved access for Canadian exports to the Australian market, and should make an important contribution to a further strengthening of the trading relations between our two countries.

ANNOUNCEMENT OF PUBLICATION OF NEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to announce the publication of a new manual or a guide entitled "Organization of the Government of Canada", or in French "L'Administration federale du Canada". It contains detailed information on the organization of the federal government, including lists of members of the cabinet, the Senate and the House of Commons, judges and officials of the supreme and exchequer courts of Canada and of the territorial courts of the Yukon and Northwest Territories and top officials of the various departments, boards and agencies of the public service.
Numerous inquiries and requests received during the last few years by the queen's printer from the public, particularly businessmen, university professors and students, have indicated the need for a publication of this kind, where can be found information which

The Budget-Economic Forecasts is incomplete or difficult to find in other government publications. I venture to say that it is expected to be quite useful to government officials as well as to the public.
The project was first studied and recommended by an interdepartmental committee established by the previous administration, which comprised representatives of the departments of the Secretary of State and of Public Printing and Stationery and the privy council office, the treasury board office and the public archives. After authority for it was given by the cabinet of the day, editing and revision of the text were entrusted to a committee of representatives of the Department of the Secretary of State, the Department of Justice and the privy council office. Incidentally, considerable revision became necessary twice in the course of the preparation and proof-printing as a result of the last two general elections.
There is a bilingual edition for free distribution to those entitled thereto under the regulations governing distribution of government publications, and separate English and French editions for sale to the public. I might add that the queen's printer already has approximately 1,000 orders for this publication, which he is now starting to fill.

[Mr. Courtemanche.l

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I took it that you would be reading the terms of the motion to the house, but you called on the hon. member for Assiniboia. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BUDGET FORECASTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes. The hon. member simply moved his motion, and I think he should indicate why he feels it is an urgent matter. I would also be glad to hear other members as to the urgency of the matter, which is the important issue at the moment. I would ask the hon. member not to proceed with the motion but to confine himself to the question of whether the house should entertain the matter at this time.

subtopic: BUDGET FORECASTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I feel that this matter is urgent because disclosure has just been made, and this is the first opportunity we have had to ask for a full debate on the question. The reason we ask for a full debate is our belief, after having heard the budget statement of the Minister of Finance and after having read extracts from the report in the Toronto Star of yesterday, that the house and the people of Canada have been misled by the forecasts of the Minister of Finance. They have been misled by his forecast that inflationary pressures are no longer of great importance, as found on page 1234 of Hansard of June 17, and his forecast of an increase of 2 per cent in the gross national product.
Because of these great discrepancies we feel that the house is entitled to an explanation from the government at this time with respect to why these forecasts were not based on the report, and why these forecasts vary so greatly from the advice given the government by its economic experts. We believe this secret document, which has been referred to in the house so often, should now be disclosed immediately because it has already appeared in the press, and because of the well known attitude of the Prime Minister in the past toward the disclosure of such reports.
We believe there is a question of privilege involved affecting the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I take it that you are passing at the moment on the question of whether there is urgency of debate as applied to this matter within the rules and practice of this house. My hon. friend is asking you to regard this as a definite matter of urgent public importance requiring debate at this particular time. In my respectful submission, Mr. Speaker, the motion not only does not fall within the accepted requirements in relation to such a motion but falls very far short of them.
If my hon. friend wishes to introduce this matter into the discussions of the house he will have an opportunity to do so only two days from now, because a supply motion is to be moved on Monday and any hon. member who regards this as a matter meriting the attention of the house will have full opportunity, I take it, to introduce it, if in order, on that motion.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is another question which applies to the motion here. The hon. member for Assiniboia seems to be leading up to the point, certainly it was evident in his remarks this morning, of alleging that a certain report which the government received from its advisers should be placed before the house. You, Mr. Speaker, have already had that same question before you and it is standing on the order paper at the present time. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate brought in such a motion about one month ago calling for the production of the same document.
When the discussion opened on that motion for production you ruled that it was not open to debate. Then, following further discussion on the point of order, you ruled that the motion could not be pressed at that point to a vote, and the mover of the motion asked that it be transferred to "Notices of Motions". There it stands now, and will stand until it is reached in the ordinary course. It is to be found on page 16 of today's order paper, item No. 46:
June 18-Mr. Pickersgill-That an order of the house do issue for a copy of "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958" as prepared by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
It is evidently the same document that the hon. member for Assiniboia is asking to have produced today. It is quite obvious, Mr. Speaker, in view of the previous proceedings in this house with regard to the same matter and the fact that the question is pending before the house on the order paper, that the motion is out of order on that ground.
There is one further observation I should like to make without trespassing into the
The Budget-Economic Forecasts realm of the merits of the issue which the hon. member for Assiniboia is seeking to raise. It seems to be implicit in his argument that this is a matter of urgent public importance, that there is some obligation upon the government in relation to advice of certain kinds that it receives from certain officials.
Let me make it quite clear that whatever use the government makes of advice from whatever source, whether advisers within the government or without, the government takes the responsibility for the views it puts before the house; and the government has taken responsibility, and full responsibility, for the views upon which the budget was based when it was introduced in this house on June 17.
Let there be no question about that. The government is not under any obligation to follow the views of any particular official or any particular adviser-

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):

However, that is not the question we are debating at the moment; it is the urgency and importance of this particular matter.
There is, I believe, no question about the importance of this matter, because an economic analysis was given by the Minister of Finance when he introduced his budget, and he based his calculations on certain statistics. Those have now, in part at least, been rejected by a government report which has, in part, been made public. Quotations from that report have appeared in the press, and they deny the validity of some of the minister's own calculations in the production of his budget. The Budget-Economic Forecasts Surely it is urgent that this matter should be cleared up. However, Mr. Speaker, if you decide that the urgency is not such as to require a debate at this moment, then surely the urgency for making this report public now has been abundantly demonstrated.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BUDGET FORECASTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I take it that the matter that is sought to be brought before the house is not the production of "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958", although the last clause in the motion rather indicates that that is sought. There is on the order paper a motion with respect to that report. I shall deal with this motion as a motion to discuss as a matter of definite urgent public importance the discrepancies between the economic forecast made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech and the forecast made to the government by its economic advisers in "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958", as outlined in the recently partially disclosed alleged extract from this report.
As the Leader of the Opposition says, there is no doubt that the economic forecast of the Minister of Finance is a matter of great public importance. However, I think the house must bear in mind, as was pointed out by the Minister of Finance, that it will have an opportunity on Monday, when a supply motion is to be moved, to make a motion relating to any matter that has not yet been decided by the house. On that account I think the urgency would have to be of such an extreme nature that it could not wait over the week end.
In this motion there does not appear to be anything of that kind. In fact it seems doubtful that the motion itself is the kind that can be introduced under rule 26, because it attempts to deal with opinions. The Minister of Finance makes a forecast, which is a matter of opinion. There is a report by the economic advisers, which is another matter of opinion. If the conflict of opinions is the sort of urgent matter which the house must debate immediately and suspend all its other business until it does so, it seems to me that we would get into hopeless confusion.
I therefore cannot accept this motion as a proper one under rule 26.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to answer the question which was addressed to me on Wednesday, July 30, by the hon. member for Lambton West dealing with water diversion at Chicago. My answer to his question, which was directed to three main points, is as follows:
1.	The position taken by Canada with respect to a proposed additional diversion of
1,000	cubic feet per second from lake Michigan at Chicago is set forth in an aide memoire dated January 6, 1958. As the document is somewhat long, I ask leave to have it printed as an annex to Hansard.

Inquiries of the Ministry
2.	To the extent that any additional diversion of water may take place at Chicago, the level of the lower lakes and connecting channels will be reduced as far as Montreal, and there will be a corresponding reduction in the availability of water for hydroelectric generation at Niagara, Barnhart and Beauharnois. The effect, however, varies at different places and at different times over a period of years. I should be pleased to arrange for the hon. member to consult tables and graphs in order to determine precisely what effect a particular diversion would have at a specific time in a specific place.
3.	Principles applicable to a diversion from lake Michigan would not necessarily apply to boundary waters, as lake Michigan is not a boundary water.

If I understood the hon. member correctly he wanted to know about the educational support supplied by the Legion?

No. At one time the Canadian Legion had a whole set of educational correspondence courses for members of the armed services, and I think they have been carried on under the minister's department for a number of years.

57071-3-1904
Supply-Veterans Affairs last January or February? I refer to the amendment whereby world war I veterans would qualify for war veterans allowance after having served a certain period overseas. How many applications have been approved since then, and what is the total annual cost?

Item agreed to.

492. To provide for the cost of administration of Veterans' Land Act; Soldier Settlement and British Family Settlement, $5,249,350.

I want to make a few brief remarks with regard to policy under this item because, while we had ample opportunity to question the director of the Veterans' Land Act administration when considering the estimates in the standing committee naturally of course we have to deal with any change of policy in the house. I wish to bring up again the old hardy perennial that I have brought before the house quite a number of times and with regard to which the minister was kind enough to support me on two or three occasions in years past. I refer to the necessity for a reduction of the acreage to a quarter of an acre for small holdings under the Veterans' Land Act.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
The matter is of primary concern to a number of veterans I have the honour to represent owing to the nature of the country and the difficulty in obtaining the acreage required under the present regulations. Before proceeding, I may say that I find that the vast majority of veterans prefer to operate under the Veterans' Land Act administration rather than under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The day they are transferred from the shepherding of the Veterans' Land Act administration to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is a sad day for them. There is a somewhat different approach to these problems on the part of the two organizations. I think that is understandable in view of the fact that the V.L.A. staff are all veterans and understand the particular problems veterans have, their psychology and their approach to things in general.
I mention the matter again at the request of a good number of veterans in my constituency and branches of the Canadian Legion. In view of the representations made in the house and in view of the minister's sympathy for our approach to this question in years past, I would ask the minister whether the government has given consideration to a reduction of the acreage for small holdings to about a quarter of an acre where the particular circumstances in any area indicate that this is desirable.

I want to thank the hon. member for bringing this matter to the attention of the house. I might advise him that it is receiving very careful consideration. We are studying the Veterans' Land Act in the department and it is our opinion that the act, being one of the most important pieces of veterans legislation, should receive study next year by the veterans affairs committee.
I think it will be realized that there are a number of amendments that could be made. The hon. member for Kootenay West will have an opportunity to present his views when this measure is under study next year. I assure him that we intend to make a very thorough study of the Veterans' Land Act next year in the veterans affairs committee. It is one of the first acts I intend to bring before it.
I hope I am there to deny some of the pessimistic views that have been expressed by some of the officials with regard to the life expectancy of veterans of the first world war.

May I take advantage of this item to pay my tribute, on behalf of this

party, to the effective, intelligent and understanding way in which this act is being administered, and especially to the works of the administration.

I should like to thank the Leader of the Opposition for his remarks. At the same time I should like also to thank the hon. member for Kootenay West, who in his remarks last night paid tribute not only to those who administer the Veterans' Land Act but to the officials who are administering all the different branches of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I appreciate those remarks, and I want to say that I personally feel they were well deserved.

Item agreed to.

I should like to speak very briefly on item No. 494 with regard to the Veterans' Land Act and the advisability of raising the ceiling on loans made under that act. I was happy to hear the minister say that this act would be brought up for consideration and amendment next session. I feel it would be wise, however, to give the committee certain information on this particular point.
As hon. members no doubt know, the ceiling for loans under the Veterans' Land Act has been set at $9,000, whereas in the case of the farm loan board it has been set at $15,000. Since the inception of the Veterans' Land Act there has been a total of something in the neighbourhood of $370 million in circulation, and at the present date there is a little more than $201 million in circulation. This is being repaid at the rate of $20,355,000 a year. There is a very negligible amount of money, $11,300, outstanding in principal and interest for more than a three-year period, and about $8,000 of this is in the province of Saskatchewan. I might add also that the province of Saskatchewan has a higher rate of cash repayment.
Because of the very low figure, and the efficiency of the program in the farming industry, I should like to ask the minister to take into consideration the advisability of raising the ceiling on loans under this act. I believe it is not necessary for me to mention a figure, because I am not one to judge the cost of establishing farms. I imagine that a sum in the neighbourhood of $20,000 would be a reasonable limit in view of the current cost of establishment. I noticed that according

to the Canadian farm loan board the demand for money today is 306 per cent greater than at the time of the inception of that board. I would ask the minister to give this matter serious consideration in the future.

I want to thank the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, Mr. Chairman, for his suggestion. I am very happy to be able to advise him that we have already prepared considerable material in the department on this very subject matter. As a matter of fact the material we have prepared is being studied not only by the Department of Agriculture but also by the Department of Finance in relation to the farm loan act. This is a matter which will be thoroughly discussed, I may tell the hon. member, in the veterans affairs committee when we have the Veterans' Land Act before that committee next year. I hope the hon. member will be a member of that committee next year as he has been this year.

Has there been any increase in the gratuities given to world war I veterans? At the time they were treated according to the standards of the day following the first world war, and have those gratuities been increased since?

The gratuities which were given to the soldiers in world war I; I think at the time they were calculated on the cost of living after the first war, and have they been increased since?

The value of the gratuity at that time was, of course, 100 per cent, and there would be no reason for increasing it now because these veterans have been reestablished for a good many years.

I just want to say a word or two on this item. I do not know whether or not I am strictly in order. I intended to say this on the administration item but it slipped my mind. In the committee we heard representations with respect to the merchant seamen. Mr. Heide suggested certain improvements concerning pensions, requested burnt-out pensions, dealt with medical boards and the extension of the Veterans' Land Act to certain seamen, and so on.
As a long-time member of the committee I realize all the complications and difficulties in doing justice to those within this group who should receive some consideration. I am primarily concerned with the individuals who may suffer some injustice at the present time because of the failure of the legislation to properly give them the protection or compensation they should have. We heard these representations from Mr. Heide, and I believe the departmental officials are going to secure some further information so we will have the representations of Mr. Heide and the information from the department to study.
I trust that at the next session the standing committee will have an opportunity to go into this matter thoroughly. I fully appreciate that the question is most complicated and difficult. In addition, although the Canadian corps of firefighters have not made representations as a body, I know that individual units or locals have written to various members in this house. Therefore I trust that at the next session the standing committee will have an opportunity to hear any representations that organization wishes to make.
Now, before I take my seat, I want to remedy an oversight on my part. In my hurry last night I forgot to express the appreciation of this group for the admirable way in which the chairman of the standing committee on veterans affairs performed his duties. We thought he was most fair in dealing with the questions that came up, and I simply want to say that so people will know that when we appreciate the way things are handled we say so, as we are not backward in saying when we think things are handled badly.

The hon. member realizes that this is not a new subject. It has been considered in veterans affairs committees for quite a number of years, ever since the second world war as a matter of fact.
3014	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs
I know he will agree with me that it has always received very sympathetic study from all members of the committee from all parties and at all times. He will recall that there was quite a stand taken, right after the war to have the merchant marine considered as a fourth arm of the service, as it were. This was not done but it concerned, I think, the Department of National Defence more than it does the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Everyone realizes the great work that was done by the merchant marine during the war. The casualties were heavy. The men were in constant danger. We all remember the trips they took to Murmansk and across the various oceans and the seven seas constantly threatened by submarines. However, what applies to the Canadian merchant marine applied also to the merchant marine of all the allied forces. I might say that none of the nations-including Great Britain, France, Australia, the United States, Italy and others -ever accepted the merchant marine as a fourth arm of the service. I think that is correct. It has not been done in Canada either.
There were a good many advantages given to the merchant marine under the war pensions act. I should like to read to the committee just some of the benefits which were granted to the merchant marine after the last war.
1.	Any seaman eligible for either the war service bonus or the special bonus was also eligible for railway fare from port to final discharge in Canada to the permanent residence of the seaman in Canada.
2.	Pensions were awarded on a scale approximating the rate in the pensions act, and were granted for death or disability suffered as a result of enemy action or counteraction. Payments are authorized under the provisions of the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act and include payment to widows and dependents of seamen killed in enemy action.
3.	Full benefits under the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act were granted.
4.	Treatment was provided for non-pensionable disabilities incurred in service at sea for a period of 18 months if evidenced within 12 months of termination of service.
5.	Compensation with pay for loss of effects and wages and payment of special bonus was continued if in enemy prison.
6.	If pensionable, treatment is provided for pensionable disabilities including hospital allowance.
7.	If pensionable, benefits under the Veterans' Land Act were available.
[Mr. Brooks.l

8.	Benefits of the Veterans Insurance Act are available to any seaman eligible for either war service bonus or special bonus.
9.	The Unemployment Insurance Act was made applicable to merchant seamen to whom the war service bonus or special bonus are payable.
There were other benefits requested and, as the hon. member mentioned, the officials of my department are meeting the veterans affairs committee and this matter is going to be discussed at the next meeting of that committee.
While I am on my feet may I say this. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo made some remarks the other night and asked some questions with reference to the War Veterans' Allowance Act, or at least with reference to making Great Britain a theatre of war for the first war. He wanted to know why it was that a period of 365 days was required. It is not necessary for me to tell the house the history of the War Veterans' Allowance Act but I might mention a few facts.
It was granted first on the recommendation of some very prominent men in the Legion and in public life in Canada and in parliament. The basis for the recommendation was the fact that the men who served in the front line trenches-and these men had been visited by those who made the recommendation-put up with the privations which they had to encounter there. Those who were in the front line in the first war know that not only were the Germans a few yards away but that there were the lice, the rats and the mud to be contended with.
I think this was first mentioned in Saint John at a meeting of the dominion command of the Canadian Legion. I believe Dr. Mac-Laren who was a former minister of pensions and national health was one of those who made the following suggestion, and Senator Power who was also at the meeting supported it. It was suggested that the terrible hardships which these men had to undergo in the first world war must have shortened their life possibly to the extent of 10 years.
That is the basis, Mr. Chairman, for providing war veterans allowances for men of the first war. It has been extended since. It was extended to dual veterans, men who had served in two world wars. It was extended to take in all men who had served in England, just recently by our amendment, except those who had not been there for 365 days.
I might give the basis for the 365 days. As to the men who landed in England in the early part of the war, many of them were well-experienced men and they were needed to drill troops and for administration purposes. They also had to put up with many

privations. We all read of the winter they spent on Salisbury Plain and know that the accommodation was not good. We also know that these men were away from their families and their homes for three and four years, whereas the men who only served for a short time and came to England-many of them, I know from reading their applications, some thousands of them-came just a few months before the war ended.
These men are not considered, and I do not think that anyone can so consider them, in the same category as the men I have just mentioned. They were home. Many of them received good wages in factories and so on. They came just at the end of the war.
In his argument last night my hon. friend said they sailed across the Atlantic ocean, and anybody who sailed across the Atlantic ocean was in great danger. I hope my hon. friend will never mention that argument before a group of these old soldiers I spoke of a few moments ago who served in the trenches amid the mud, lice, rats and so on with the Germans in front of them.
Mind you, if the late arrivals had suffered I would be the first one to ask that they receive this benefit. But in the latter part of the war the Atlantic ocean was not too dangerous to cross. The German navy had been destroyed. There were very few U-boats. There was no great danger in going across the Atlantic ocean in 1918, just before the war ended. As a matter of fact those who took that trip stayed a few months in England and came back again. It would certainly take some stretch of the imagination to make me or any of the members of the veterans organizations across this country believe that the lives of those men had been reduced by 10 years or 10 months or even by 10 days.
That, Mr. Chairman and hon. members, is my opinion and I think it is the opinion of most of the veterans across this country, namely that there is no necessity for extending the war veterans allowance benefits any further than we have extended them, namely to the extent of 365 days in England.
The hon. member spoke about the Newfoundland veterans and I have assured him, as I assure him once again, that this is one of the first matters with which I am hoping to deal. It takes a little time, and I perhaps get a little impatient. I thought we might have attended to this matter before now, but it does take longer than we amateurs expect when we try to do these things. It is, however, being thoroughly studied and is well on the way.
The hon. member also mentioned a Newfoundland hospital, and I think he suggested that the hospital at Fort Pepperrell might
Supply-Veterans Affairs be acquired. Several weeks ago we became aware of the possibility that this hospital would be vacated by the United States forces and might become available for other use. Consideration was given to the usefulness of this hospital to the Department of Veterans Affairs. It is not intended to request that this hospital be turned over to the department, since it is considered that the proposal already made for the construction of hospital accommodation in St. John's will provide better and more efficient facilities for the hospitalization of veterans in Newfoundland. I also understand that the problem of getting doctors and nurses would create considerable difficulty.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words in reply to the statement the minister has just made. I think everyone would agree with the stand taken when the war veterans allowance was introduced, which was that by reason of his war service in the trenches and the hardships undergone by the serviceman, his normal span of life was reduced by about 10 years, and he would therefore require a pension at the age of 60 because his physical condition would be comparable with that of an ordinary person at the age of 70. Pensions at that time, however, were available only to people aged 70 and over and it was felt that something should be done for the veterans. This was carried out by means of the burned-out pension or the war veterans' allowance.
I am in complete agreement with the minister up to that point, but as he himself pointed out, as time went on these restrictions became relaxed, and pensions were awarded on the basis of a person having served in a theatre of war. That theatre of war was anywhere on the continent of Europe. Many people who went overseas in 1917 and arrived on the continent after the armistice, without having spent a day in the trenches and without having heard a shot fired, but simply because they were lucky enough to get across the channel and land in France, immediately became eligible under the act for a burned-out pension.
Many such people have received awards, and this introduces an element of inequity in the administration of this legislation. If the benefits were restricted to only those people who had served in the firing line and who had undergone hardships and privations such as the rats-the minister mentioned rats but he did not mention vermin, although I can assure him they were worse than the rats in my part of the line-

I shall never forget them.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

-that would have been perfectly all right, but we have gone away from that idea and have said that anybody who got to Europe at any time gets a war veterans allowance. I know of many cases of people who, just because they were lucky enough to get a draft in the last months of the war, are in this position. I also know so far as the Newfoundland regiment was concerned, those soldiers were pushed across pretty fast and were in England for perhaps three or four days and then were across the channel. Many became eligible for war veterans allowance after world war I who were not away from their families as long as a lot of other people; some were away for 365 days.
But my quarrel with this is the basis upon which it is awarded. That basis is that the man must have served in a theatre of war, and I contend that in the year 1917 the Atlantic ocean was every bit as much a theatre of war as was the continent of Europe at the time of the armistice.
If a soldier went across in 1917 he would have his year. I was speaking of 1918.

I mentioned the latter part of the year. The minister made one statement which I want to refute right away. He said that he thought there would be quite a great deal of trouble in convincing the old sweats that there was much danger in crossing the Atlantic ocean. I would like to tell him that when I crossed that ocean the submarine menace was pretty bad.

When did you cross? Let us get this matter straightened out. I was speaking of the latter part of 1918 after the German navy had been driven off the seas and the submarines had mostly been destroyed. I know that in the first three years of the war it was very dangerous to cross the ocean, but all those men are eligible for war veterans' allowance. Do not let us get confused. When did the hon. member cross the ocean?
I crossed early in 1917.
Oh, certainly.

But I am referring to the people who came after that time, and I do not think the subs were chased off the ocean to that extent, even in 1918. Nineteen hundred and seventeen, if I remember correctly, was the height of the sub menace. That was the hardest time. This brings to mind another inequity, in that a merchant navy man who enlisted in 1918 and served on an escort for these fellows who were going over gets credit for having served in a theatre of war and receives a war


veterans allowance. The poor devil who was on the ship being escorted, however, cannot get a war veterans allowance because he was not in a theatre of war. I think that inequity should be straightened out.
I was very glad to hear the minister state that certain proposals are being considered for a veterans' hospital in Newfoundland which would be much better than the facilities offered by the United States base at Fort Pepperrell. I wonder if the minister could go a step further and tell us just what proposals are under consideration.
I may say the proposals are not yet final. As soon as they are I will let the hon. member know.
Item agreed to.
