speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Department of Justice, vote No. 373. This item will be found on page 71 of the blue book, the details on page 499. Shall the item carry?
Mr. Chairman, is the minister going to give us any statement on this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it had not been my intention to do so and I do not think that has been the custom in the past. I shall be very glad to listen to any general observations members may have to make and attempt to reply to any questions of a general nature on this item with respect to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few observations on one specific subject, and that is the security screening which is carried on-of course by and under the responsibility of the government-and of which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is the principal instrument. I noted with a great deal of interest the answer given by the minister to a question put by the hon. member for Port Arthur which will be found at page 831 of Hansard for June 4, 1958. Perhaps in order to refresh the memories of members of the committee I might read both the question and the answer.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to address this question to the Minister of Justice. In view of the welcome news that a new federal approach to security was revealed in a C.B.C. versus labour dispute involving an employee, would the minister care to make a statement to

this house on the scope of the new federal approach in allowing adverse security reports to be seen by those reported upon?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should at once correct the misapprehension which would otherwise be created by the form in which the question was put. To my knowledge, at the hearing which was arranged as a special hearing in this one case, the written security reports, at least in the sense of the complete documents on file, were not shown to the employee involved. It would not be possible to disclose our security files to anyone not authorized to see them.
This particular procedure was an attempt to find an answer to the problem of allowing a hearing, which could properly be called a hearing, to an employee who is suspected on security grounds. In so far as the hearing went, it was a special arrangement, and we are continuing to study the whole question to see if this does suggest a suitable pattern for dealing with this problem.
I read that statement not to criticize it in any way whatsoever. When the Minister of Justice was on this side of the house on several occasions-and I will not waste the time of the committee by referring to them now-he expressed concern about the security procedures which were in effect at that time, and I certainly feel that any hon. member who does not feel concerned about this subject is not really sensitive to the fundamental concepts of justice.
As members of the committee know, I have had over 20 years' experience in the public service and in public life, and it so happens that in the past I have had a good deal to do with such matters in one way or another and in one capacity or another, and I can assure hon. members that there is no more difficult and no more disagreeable public duty which anyone has to perform than that performed by whoever is responsible for carrying out these procedures. It is, I think, distasteful to the natural sense of justice of all of us that any kind of circumstance should arise where a man should be deprived of his employment, or transferred, as often happens, from one kind of employment to another, for reasons which are not fully disclosed to that person. It is repugnant to all of us, or at least I hope it is. It was certainly very repugnant to me.
The only justification I considered to exist when I was where the hon. gentleman is now, on the treasury benches, for having any such procedure, is that it is the supreme duty of the government to safeguard the state itself, and that in the kind of world in which we have had the misfortune to live for a very long time-I say "misfortune" from a somewhat limited point of view, because I do not really think it is a misfortune to be alive, but in the kind of world in which we have had the misfortune to have had to carry on our public affairs-we have been faced at least for 20 years with enemies or potential
Supply-R.C.M.P.
enemies of the Canadian people who have sought to undermine the security of our country both in war and in the postwar period, and we had a very deplorable experience which is not yet out of the memories of many of us, immediately after the war, when it was discovered, by a series of accidents, coupled with excellent police work, that there were in various branches of the public service certain persons who appeared to be, and some of them were convicted of being, the agents of a country which, at least, had no friendly designs in having those agents there.
Therefore, it seems to me there is no way in which the government can escape its responsibility for security screening. As hon. members know, I am not very lavish in my compliments to hon. gentlemen opposite, but I have been very much impressed by the responsible attitude displayed by the Minister of Justice in this matter since he has occupied his present position. He has never attempted to pretend that every position he took when he was over here has turned out to be a tenable position. He has honestly and frankly stated the difficulties he found when he assumed his responsibilities, and he has tried to face this problem squarely.
If these people were guilty of some kind of crime, that would be very simple to deal with. A charge could be laid in the courts and the whole matter disposed of. But what really is the problem in the case of security is that all there is, is suspicion, suspicion that a man is not reliable. That does not mean he is a spy, but that he is thought to be the kind of person who, because of his habits or associations, might betray the interests of our country in essential respects.
The main debate about this subject is really narrowed down to a small point, and that point is this; whether, when such a man is suspected, he should be told precisely what the suspicion is, or whether he should not. This is the whole problem. We have had a good many debates in this house in which arguments have been raised on both sides of that question. The subject has been debated in Westminster also, and in neither Canada nor in the United Kingdom-I do not propose to go further afield for any examples, because I do not think any of the other examples have been very helpful-has it been found possible by the government, whatever its political complexion, to make all the information and all the allegations available to the suspected person in order that he might have an opportunity to reply to them fully, or to refute them.
That is what we should like to do. I hope everyone in the committee would like to see that done if it could be done, but I want to

Supply-R.C.M.P.
emphasize again that these people are not being charged with any crime, and the consequences of making information available to such a person could be manifold, if the suspicions were justified. There is the risk that if he is in guilty association he will inform the persons with whom he has that association. Another consequence could arise, particularly if the man did not feel any sense of guilt; with the natural indignation that all of us would feel in such a situation he might make the whole matter public.
I may be asked why I am concerned about that, now that I am no longer in the government, but I would say this. If, indeed, there be a good case for dispensing with the services of a man on security grounds, that is no reason for making him unemployable. But if a great public inquiry is aroused, what one is really doing is injuring the long-term prospects of the man himself for gainful and useful employment and for a quiet life, a man who is not guilty of any crime but who might be indiscreet. Now, this is, as I say, the problem. I know the minister feels the same concern that we felt when we were on the treasury benches to meet this problem in the best way it can be met.
The minister not only excited my curiosity but he also raised a point which I think should be of concern to all of us in the answer he gave on June 4. I was hoping that, after any other hon. members who wished to say anything about this particular aspect of the subject have spoken, the minister would tell us whether any progress has been made along this line, or whether any other changes have been made in the procedures that were followed.
Does the minister want to answer that before we speak on another subject?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If no other hon. member wishes to speak on this subject I can perhaps deal with it at this time. I appreciate what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has said, both with respect to myself and the efforts made and the position taken by this government in connection with this matter in following out the desire to establish a satisfactory procedure. I like to think that perhaps some of the feelings now reflected in the remarks of the hon. gentleman on this subject have been instilled in his breast by the fact that he is now a student of law and because-
I was a student of liberty long ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-of that perhaps it may be fair to suggest that he has a livelier or at least perhaps a more perceptive sense and appreciation of the implications of this subject than when he was not a student of law.

I agree with him at once about the difficulty of the situation. I do not think I have to take issue with anything he said, or particularly anything that he attributed as having been said by me when I was in opposition; but I think I should make it clear that at all times when I was on that side of the house and took part in discussions of this question I never went any further than to say that the man should be given some sort of hearing if some satisfactory method could be devised. I believe it will be found, on checking the record, that I was always careful not to go so far as to say that sources of information should be disclosed to him.
I think the hon. gentleman is quite correct and I have no quarrel with him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When we took office we were concerned to see how far we could go in implementing the principle that we had enunciated, namely that it would be desirable to arrange that a person in the public service, suspect on security grounds, would be given a hearing at which he might get some indication of the nature of the suspicions against him; to see if we could arrange that sort of hearing and yet not have to go all the way and disclose such facts as would in fact compromise your security sources. We undertook that study, and we found ourselves quite early confronted with a particular case, which was the case referred to earlier by the hon. gentleman and which was the subject of question and answer on June 4, as recorded on page 831 of Hansard.
There is, I think, one modification I should make in what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said with regard to the situation in this country and the United Kingdom. He said, as I took down his words, "Neither in Canada nor in the United Kingdom has it been found possible to make all the allegations or all the information available to the suspected person." With these words in their literal sense I have no disagreement, but it is a fact that the United Kingdom went further than we did with respect to giving the suspected person a form of hearing.
That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They had a committee which was set up. This will all be found reported in the United Kingdom debates of, I think, about five or six years ago, which I think the hon. gentleman has studied, as I did.
If the minister will permit me, it was just by inadvertence that I did not go on to point that out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I accept that completely, but I say the significant difference between our

procedure and the procedure in the United Kingdom is this. They had set up a system under which there was a hearing granted to the suspected person. It was made clear that all he would receive was a general indication of the sort of grounds of suspicion, that is, only an indication of the nature of the case against him, the government reserving always to itself the right to decide how far disclosure would be made. And at that hearing which, as I recall it, is conducted by a panel of retired civil servants-
That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-the accused-that is the danger one gets into, the suspected person- I would like almost to expunge that word from Hansard, because he is not an accused person-the suspected person is not accompanied by counsel. When we took over, however, we wanted to see how far we could go in this direction, which was the sort of direction we had advocated when we were in opposition.
I must say also, to complete the picture here and in fairness to the former administration, that in the discussion that did take place in the house when they were here and we were over there the former prime minister made it clear that they had thoroughly studied the English system and the system in the United States-I think he went that far-[DOT] and while they admitted that the British system went a little further than ours, they felt that ours was preferable and they decided not to adopt the British system.
That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
However, as I say, when we took office we immediately commenced a study to see how far we could go, what modifications we should introduce along those lines. We were confronted with this case in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which had commenced by way of a grievance brought by an employee who had been refused a promotion to which he felt he was entitled and to which the union of which he was a member felt he was entitled. There had been a special board of inquiry appointed to arbitrate this grievance, and they soon found that there was a reluctance on the part of the C.B.C. to indicate the real nature of the reasons why this promotion had been refused.
In any event, it soon became obvious to the chairman of the board, as I recall it; the question was put to him in such a form that it finally became apparent there was a security aspect involved. I think it is fair to say that there the situation pretty well bogged down, because there was no procedure for dealing with the situation that was then disclosed.
Supply-R.C.M.P.
Obviously the arbitration board which had been appointed to investigate a labour dispute could not assert jurisdiction over the question of security.
I know there was correspondence and discussion between the chairman of the board and my predecessor, but no solution of the difficulty had been found when we took office. So we were faced with a situation quite soon-well, in fact immediately-after June 10 of last year. In the discussions with the officials concerned and with my advisers in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has pointed out, are the main advisers to the government in the field of security, I outlined to them my view with regard to this matter of a hearing. They indicated to me all the difficulties and dangers which they felt in the matter and which had been made clear, I think, in the remarks of the hon. gentleman, namely the difficulty of giving a hearing which would be a hearing in substance and not only in form, the danger that you might disclose, and thus compromise, some vital security information, particularly with regard to the sources of that information. But it was felt that at least on an experimental basis in this particular case we would be justified in arranging a hearing.
Accordingly, with the approval of cabinet a special commissioner was appointed. I will not go into all the terms of reference, but we did our best to devise a system, a form of hearing, under which it would be made possible for the commissioner to disclose to the suspected man at least the general nature of the grounds of suspicion, the kind of thing of which he was suspected, and give him a chance to answer. The representative of the union and the representatives of the C.B.C. expressed themselves as satisfied with the formula we devised, as did the security advisers of the government, and the hearing was accordingly arranged and held with results that have been reported and are now public knowledge.
I should now revert to the general situation. Discussions were initiated with other departments and the ministers concerned, particularly in what may be described as the vital departments in this matter of security, and finally an interdepartmental panel was requested to go into the whole matter. I am not going to minimize the difficulties for a moment. We found that there were difficulties to which as yet we have not found an answer; that is, difficulties in the way of applying the procedure which was made applicable in a specific case to all the general run of problems that may arise in connection with this subject of adverse

Supply-R.C.M.P.
security reports on persons in the public service. As I said in the house on June 4, "in so far as the hearing went", referring to the specific hearing in the C.B.C. case, "it was a special arrangement and we are continuing to study the whole question to see if this does not suggest a suitable pattern for dealing with this problem."
The answer I must now give to the question raised by the hon. member as to what is the present position must be confined to saying that it is my feeling that we have found a pattern which, with some modification and some limitations, may be capable of expansion and of more general application than to the one individual case, but I am not able to say that we have yet found a pattern that can be applied to all cases that may arise in this field. We are continuing the study.
Would the minister care to indicate the general lines of the procedure, or are they so similar to those followed in this particular case that it really covers it? The minister referred to a pattern.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The general lines of procedure we have in mind to apply would, I think, be somewhat similar to the formula in that case. The question would be to what areas of the government service you extend it and also what rights of representation does the individual have. It is a matter of record- the order in council was published-that in this particular case the person had the right to be accompanied by counsel. My hon. friend will appreciate that that goes further than the British system. One question we are studying now, and a very important one, is whether that right should be made general if we do apply this procedure to more cases, or to what extent the right of representation might be allowed.

There is another aspect of the subject about which I should like to make one or two observations and pose one or two questions. As a foundation for that I think perhaps the simplest thing I can do is to refer the committee to a question asked by the hon. member for Skeena to which the minister gave an answer on July 8, as appears at page 2047 of Hansard. The question asked was as follows:
1.	Does the R.C.M.P. maintain any files or dossiers on members of parliament?
2.	If so, upon which members of the present parliament are such files or dossiers maintained?
The answer given by the minister was as follows:
AH Royal Canadian Mounted Police files on individuals are confidential and many are secret.
Perhaps I might interject here that I agree completely with the answer given by the minister. I am not addressing myself to this

question in so far as members of parliament or any particular group are concerned. What I am interested in is the general principle enunciated here.
One of the primary duties of all those responsible for such files is to respect and preserve the confidential or secret nature of their contents. It will be appreciated also that a large number of such files are started by reports, statements or knowledge of activities coming to the attention of responsible members of the police which they are bound to investigate in the course of their duties. The followup on such reports in many cases reveals no necessity for further action, yet there is still a file. This means that many files will be in existence under the names of individuals against whom there is nothing of a substantial, let alone a criminal, nature.
It will therefore be generally agreed that it would be grossly unfair to any such individual to have it revealed or even suspected that there exists a police file under his name, yet there may be many ways in which such a suspicion could be raised. One of the surest ways of laying the foundation for the raising of suspicion would be to isolate-
I think the rest of the answer applies specifically to members of parliament, and I would be wasting the time of the committee by reading it. I said when I started that I agree with the answer given by the minister. I am not one of those who believe in the purveying of hearsay from police reports or from any other source and the defamation of persons' characters in that way. I think it is right and proper, and indeed a fundamental duty of the government, to safeguard these files.
Of course I had a good deal of experience when I was minister of citizenship and immigration, a post which was also occupied for some time in an acting capacity by the present Minister of Justice. One of the duties, and a most disagreeable one, imposed upon the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was the duty of satisfying himself that he was not admitting to this country persons who would subsequently become a danger to the security of the state, and this involved almost daily consultation with the police and access to police files.
I see, sir, that it is one o'clock, and I should like to pursue this matter a little further.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

When we adjourned at one o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I had just put on the record part of an answer given by the minister to a question by the hon. member for Skeena, on July 8, and which referred in general terms to the principle governing the use of the files on individuals maintained by

the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In order to give some continuity to my argument, I should like to read again the first paragraph only of that answer. It is only two sentences:
All Royal Canadian Mounted Police files on individuals are confidential and many are secret. One of the primary duties of all those responsible for such files is to respect and preserve the confidential or secret nature of their contents.
I believe I had said just before we adjourned for lunch that a great many of these files or, at any rate, reports from these files, came to my attention in my official capacity when I was minister of citizenship and immigration. The most scrupulous care was taken by me and by the deputy minister, who was the only other person authorized to see these files, to make sure, not only that nothing in these files was disclosed to any unauthorized person including the persons referred to in the files, but we went to very great lengths not to disclose the fact that "security" was the reason for our failure to accept applications from persons who wished to immigrate to this country. We simply said that the application was rejected, and I was criticized quite frequently in this house for doing so, by no one perhaps more strongly than by the present Minister of Justice. As I said, I was criticized for my failure to give any reasons for these rejections.
My argument always was that if I gave reasons in all other cases-this was my principal argument but there were others-I would isolate the security cases. People would know, by a process of elimination, that the rest of the rejections were on security grounds. In order to preserve the sanctity of the files and the information-although I was acting on my own responsibility and on the advice which I thought was, on balance, sound that I should do this-the course I have outlined was followed. I am not seeking to enter into any argument about the practice in the department of immigration; that would be quite unfair to the minister and to the committee. I am merely citing this as an example of how scrupulous I was, and I think this was true of all my colleagues who had to do with these matters, in the use of these police files and police reports.
I say again that I agree with what the minister said in reply to the hon. member for Skeena. I do not believe that anything but harm could come from making public even the existence of files. In order to preserve organized society we have to have police forces. No doubt if we were all good, all as virtuous as we ought to be, we could dispense with the police and save quite a lot of money. But we cannot. The police have to make investigations of people who, in many cases, are innocent or, at least, not
Supply-R.C.M.P.
guilty. I prefer, I must say, the old English phrase "not guilty", because it is very hard to arrive at any accurate conception of innocence, at least in my experience.
But I think it is obvious that it will be very harmful to the character and reputation and the position in society, indeed even the economic prospects, of many people if it is known that their conduct is being investigated by the police. I believe, therefore, the minister is completely right in the position he takes that there should be no disclosure that the police have files on any person until such time as the police use these files for taking action in the courts. We know from experience, and I am quite satisfied about this, that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is a very well administered force. I doubt if there is any better administered force anywhere in the world. We know that they do not take action on trivial grounds. There is the greatest consideration given in these matters.
I was, therefore, greatly perturbed, and I think that many hon. member were greatly perturbed, by something which happened in this committee a day or two ago when we were told by one of the minister's colleagues, in relation to a particular case-perhaps in order to make clear my point I shall have to refresh the memories of hon. members about this case-the minister was being asked what information-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend is seeking to revive a matter that was discussed at great length in the committee when we were dealing with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, Mr. Chairman, may I respectfully suggest he would be out of order.
I am not seeking to do anything of the kind, sir. What I am seeking to do is to lay the foundation for a question of the minister respecting the activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Ask the question, then.

I think perhaps I can exercise my judgment as well as the minister can for me, as to the foundation I need to lay in order to ask a question in a manner to enable all hon. members to understand it. The minister need have no concern about this question if he has no feeling of guilt about the matter.
We were told that certain action was taken by the Minister of Agriculture because he had a considerable number of police and other reports from which he said he was completely satisfied that this man was guilty of securing contraband liquor from these ships. I, of course, have no means of knowing, because

Supply-R.C.M.P.
the minister refused to answer so many questions, whether these police reports to which the Minister of Agriculture referred were Reports of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. If the Minister of Justice can assure me they were not and the Minister of Agriculture had no report from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on which to base his statements, then I would feel I was out of order and would not pursue this matter any further. I would desist immediately.
If on the contrary, when the Minister of Agriculture was referring to police reports he was referring to reports from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I submit that this was an abuse of those documents, and an abuse of those documents such as in my experience there has never been before in parliament. The minister should explain how this came about. The minister told us one of the primary duties of those responsible for such files is to respect and preserve the confidential and secret nature of their contents. The question I am putting to the minister is a very simple question. Did the R.C.M.P. provide any files on this particular person to the Minister of Agriculture on which this public statement, made under his immunity in parliament, was made concerning the reputation of a man against whom no charge was laid in the criminal courts, a man who is, under our law, not guilty?
That is why I said earlier that I preferred the old English expression "not guilty" to the word "innocent" because it is extremely hard to define innocence. But under our law, under our system of justice, a man is not guilty until he has been found guilty by the courts. We had the experience here where someone under the immunity of parliament was found guilty by a member of the executive branch of government who said that he found him guilty on the basis of police reports. I was tremendously disturbed by that, Mr. Chairman. As was my duty, I did my best to find out-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must point out to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that he is at present discussing the conduct of the Minister of Agriculture in relation to the particular case to which he is referring at the present time. That procedure is quite out of order and I must ask the hon. member to limit his remarks to the estimates of the Department of Justice, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in particular.
If I have in any way transgressed the rules of the house, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I am sorry.
You have been out of order more than has any other member of the House of Commons.

I am sure that the hon.
member for Saint John-Albert is not in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member
for Bonavista-Twillingate has the floor.

It may be that I did not express myself very clearly. I will endeavour to circumscribe my observations to the limit. I am very much concerned at this time about this situation but in this committee at this time on the estimates of the Minister of Justice or of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police I am not concerned about any aspect of the conduct of the Minister of Agriculture except one. I am concerned to find out whether the Minister of Agriculture used the files of the R.C.M.P. in a manner which is certainly not consistent with the answer given to the hon. member for Skeena by the Minister of Justice. That is the only matter with which I am concerned. It seems to me that I should now leave it to the minister to tell us whether or not the Minister of Agriculture was furnished with any files, information or reports by the R.C.M.P. on the particular case which was under discussion in this house and on which the minister made what I regarded as the defamatory statements he made in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think this matter should be dealt with at once if other hon. gentlemen will permit me to do so. I think I can only echo the words used by the Minister of Agriculture that this is a classic example of making a mountain out of a molehill. It is true that, in answer to the question which has been referred to by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I said that all Royal Canadian Mounted Police files are confidential and secret and that it is the duty of those in charge of those files to preserve their confidential or secret nature; and to that I add "as the case may be".
The hon. gentleman, under the guise of concern with regard to security which we all agree is secret-and the contents of security files must be secret-has proceeded to attempt to draw an erroneous, unfair and inapplicable conclusion with regard to the use to be made of files which are confidential. I made some reference earlier to the fact that the hon. gentleman is now a student at law. I think perhaps I should now refer to the fact that he could not have been applying himself to his studies very long or he would appreciate the difference between security and secret information, and confidential information.
The simple answer to this whole matter, so far as the case referred to in Montreal is concerned, is that there was an investigation of an official of the Department of Agriculture carried on by the R.C.M.P., as a

result of which the R.C.M.P. took certain action. I do not think my hon. friend would wish to be this absurd, but he has been this absurd. He has suggested that the Minister of Agriculture should not have been shown or been informed as to the results of the police investigation into the activities of an official of that minister's department. The case is just as simple as that. It just shows the absurd lengths my hon. friend is prepared to go in his efforts to seek to revive here a discussion which properly took place-and which should only properly take place-on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to pursue this matter. The minister has made a definite allegation-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I recognize the hon. member for Vancouver East.
The minister has made a definite allegation about me.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I point out to the hon. member that I have given the floor to the hon. member for Vancouver East.

Mr. Chairman, I am raising a question of privilege, which procedure I believe is in order at any time. The Minister of Justice has just asserted that I said the Minister of Agriculture was not entitled to be shown these files. I said nothing of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was certainly the inference.

It was not what I said nor was it the inference to be taken from what I said. What I said was that the Minister of Agriculture was not entitled to make the contents of these files public in order to defame a man who was not guilty in the eyes of the law. If the Minister of Justice considers that is a principle-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member is being not only absurd but is being repetitious.
I am speaking on a question of privilege. I would ask the minister to sit down.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am raising a point of order.
I am speaking on a question of privilege and I have not concluded what I have to say. I had many lessons in procedure from the hon. gentleman when he sat over here on this side of the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. We are discussing a question which has already been discussed
Supply-R.C.M.P.
in the house. We cannot go back to the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture nor can we discuss at the present time the conduct or the behaviour of the Minister of Agriculture. Our discussion must be relevant and we must talk about the estimates of the Department of Justice. Actually, if an investigation was made by the Department of Justice, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in particular, and if the information secured from this investigation was given to the Minister of Agriculture, it is quite normal to presume that the Minister of Agriculture based his further action on the information received. But this question was all threshed out in this house at great length and I believe it is quite out of order at the present time to go back to this particular debate and for hon. members to pass judgment on the conduct of the Minister of Agriculture.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to put another question to the Minister of Justice.
Order
It is a question that has nothing to do with this particular case.
Mr. Chairman, I thought I had the floor.
It has to do with the general principles surrounding the case but not the specific matter itself.
Order.

I want to ask the minister whether he believes it is proper for himself or any other member of the government here in this house to use information secured from the confidential police files in order to defame and besmirch the character of a man who has not been tried in the courts.
Oh, oh.

You are a
privy councillor. Have you not more respect for parliament? Shame.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would not normally answer a question of that kind but I do not think it should be allowed to stand on the record by itself. In the first place, there is absolutely no justification for the terms used by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. In the second place, I would point out that the information given was requested, obtained and insisted upon by hon. members opposite.

The minister himself has not answered my question at all, Mr. Chairman. He has gone back to the case which you ruled could not be discussed. I asked a perfectly general question and I repeat it.

Supply-R.C.M.P.
Does the minister believe that the confidential files of the mounted police should be used so that a minister may make statements in this house based upon those files concerning the character and reputation of a person who has not been convicted by the courts of any offence whatsoever. That is the question I am putting to the minister. Does he think that is a proper use of the files of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police? I would remind him that such use was never made of those files in the days during which we were in office.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not believe that question is relevant to the matter under discussion at the present time.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. We are now discussing the estimates of the Department of Justice with relation to the administration of this particular department and I do not believe the question asked of the minister by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is relevant to the present discussion.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that if we cannot discuss the use made by the administration of the files of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, then there is no aspect which we can discuss. Surely the files are the product of the police administration and the purpose, the reason why we have the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, is precisely to accumulate this information, to make these investigations in order that the information may be used for the protection of society. Furthermore, surely it is a restriction upon the freedom of speech in this house to suggest for one moment that we cannot discuss the use made of these files which are paid for by the taxpayers. We are in committee of supply, appropriating or not appropriating moneys for the service of Her Majesty which is to be spent by the minister who is responsible to this house. The minister is ultimately responsible for all of these files and the use that is made of them and I have asked him a question about their use. The minister did not have any hesitation in answering the hon. member for Skeena-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no hesitation in answering the hon. member if he will just cease his tirade and give me an opportunity to do so.
I think I have the floor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course if the hon. gentleman wishes to prevent an answer from being given, that is his privilege.
Getting childish now.

I want to repeat what I said before, namely that I think this committee is entitled to know whether or not the minister considers it is a proper use of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police files to base upon them statements in this house with respect to persons who have not been found guilty of any kind of offence in the courts of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, inasmuch as this question cannot be answered in the abstract because of the efforts-and I make no comment as to whether they are proper or not-of the hon. gentleman to relate these files to an incident regarding an official of the Department of Agriculture, I have to answer the question in this way.
In this particular case no improper use was made of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police files. There was an investigation which disclosed certain facts and, as a result, an order was made by the Minister of National Revenue, acting within the proper scope of his statutory authority, for the destruction of contraband goods. That order was carried out without protest from the person affected by the order and the contraband goods were confiscated and destroyed. That is the sum and substance of that incident; there was no defamation of character and there was no improper use of Royal Canadian Mounted Police files. The order made on the authority of the Minister of National Revenue was based on information properly coming to him as a result of an R.C.M.P. investigation. That is the answer to that question.
The answer to the general question is that the hon. member knows as well as I do that of course it would not be proper to make improper use of R.C.M.P. files for the purpose of defamation of character, and no such thing has been done by this government, whatever may have been done by the former government.
Mr. Chairman, I assume that you will allow me the same liberty you have allowed the minister-
Oh, oh.

-to comment upon his remarks on this particular case. I have no quarrel whatsoever and neither would any responsible person have any quarrel with what the minister has now told us was done by the Minister of National Revenue. If the Minister of National Revenue or any officer of his department used any information secured from the mounted police in order to deal with contraband goods, that is perfectly proper. I have no objection whatsoever to that and neither would any

sensible person have any objection to it. I at no time objected to it, in fact I did not even know about it until the minister told us just now.
What I did know about, however, is that another of the minister's colleagues came into this house and boasted that he had police reports which he had never shown to the accused person-and I use the word in the same sense as did the minister because this man was never accused of anything; I would call him the defamed person-and took advantage of his immunity in this house and on the basis of these police reports blackened the character of a man who has never been allowed to stand trial and who has never even heard the charges against him, according to the admission of the Minister of Agriculture.
Order. Sit down.
And if that is justice-
Sit down.
-then it is something new.
He is a smuggler; are you trying to protect a smuggler?
No one is a smuggler until he is convicted. Perhaps the hon. gentleman convicts a person without trial.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I remind hon. members of this house that this is not the time to discuss the conduct of another minister of the crown in relation to a question which has already been discussed in the house.
We are now discussing the estimates of the R.C.M.P. and we must adhere to the administrative elements of the estimate before us, so it is quite out of order to hold a discussion on the conduct of the Minister of Agriculture in relation to this particular case which has already been mentioned.
Mr. Chairman, if the minister is content to leave the matter where it now stands, I am satisfied.

Mr. Chairman, I hope I may be permitted to discuss two matters relating to the R.C.M.P. The first matter I raise at the request of a number of members of the R.C.M.P. who, of course, shall remain unnamed but who over a period of many months have drawn to my attention a question which is disturbing many members of the service and on account of which there have been many resignations and in respect of which there are likely to be many resignations in the future. I refer to a situation of which I am certain the minister is aware, namely, the insistence of the R.C.M.P. on
Supply-R.C.M.P.
retaining a regulation which says that because you are in the scarlet and gold love goes out of the window.
I know there are many things which can be covered by law and regulation, but I have my doubts that any law or regulation can ever be formulated which will stand in the way of a man falling in love with a woman, and heaven help us if any way is ever found in which to do that. But, Mr. Chairman, this regulation has been in effect for a long time in the R.C.M.P. that once you take the oath you cannot legally express yourself as a man to a woman until you have served at least five years. A great many of the new recruits to the service are young men, and just as time after time we find that those who are not in service meet the woman of their dreams, so do the boys in scarlet and gold. But they are told: you cannot get married. Why not, Mr. Chairman?
I know that the men of the R.C.M.P. move from one municipality to another and from one province to another, but why, because of that, should a man and the woman of his choice be told: you must remain separated. What is the result? I am certain the minister knows that there is a comparatively rapid turnover in the service every year, and I feel certain he would find out, very often, that it is because of this regulation, and because the man concerned says that if he cannot get the woman of his choice by staying in the service, then he is jolly well going out of the service. That does not mean he is going to be out of a job, because I have been told that a man who has been trained in the R.C.M.P. is not going to be out of a job long after he leaves that service, because the municipalities and provinces, because of the good training he has received, are tickled to death to employ him on provincial or municipal service. I have been asked by a surprising number of members of the R.C.M.P. if I could raise this point in the House of Commons, and I ask the Minister of Justice whether he could tell us if there is going to be any change in this regulation.
Mr. Chairman, I said there was a second point which I should like to raise at this time. Unfortunately, there are some men and women who are anti-social and who break the law. Because they are anti-social they are put in jail, and this country spends a great many millions of dollars every year to keep these anti-social persons behind prison walls. In addition, we spend millions of dollars annually trying to rehabilitate these persons and give them a social conscience. Millions of dollars are spent on formal education when required, on vocational training, on psychiatric treatment and on psychologists' guidance for the purpose of rehabilitating

Supply-R.C.M.P.
these anti-social individuals. Then, after the prison term is served they are released and go back into society, and I am sure it is the hope of the Minister of Justice that they will then become social beings. I think, also, that the Minister of Justice would agree that those who have committed an offence and who have paid for their crime should not be hounded back into a criminal life.
I would be the last person to condemn the majority because of the action of a few, and I want to make it abundantly clear that in my estimation the majority of members of the R.C.M.P. do everything they possibly can to assist in the rehabilitation of former criminals who have served their sentences. Unfortunately, however, there are a few who do not have that attitude, and this is a serious matter when we remember the millions of dollars which this country is spending in endeavouring to rehabilitate antisocial persons, and when we recognize that up to the present, at least, we appear to a considerable extent to have failed in that object.
I was somewhat amazed, reading the annual report of the commissioner of penitentiaries for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1957, to see on page 53 that the percentage of recidivists in the penitentiaries that year in Canada was 80.23. It may be that the people I have just referred to constitute only part of that number, but whatever can be done in this regard should be done without delay, because men who have served their sentences and who are desirous of becoming useful members of society should not be so hounded that they cannot rehabilitate themselves. By that, I mean that they should not be stopped in public wherever they go by members of the police force.
At this moment I am discussing the R.C.M.P. If they get a job, it should not be felt to be the responsibility of the R.C.M.P.-and I repeat that I am only speaking now, of a very small minority-to go to that man's employer and say: do you know you have a former criminal in your employment? The result nine times out of ten is that the man loses his job, and when that happens more than once hon. members will realize the effect upon the man concerned who must have been somewhat weak-minded to have become a criminal in the first place.
I want to tell the Minister of Justice and the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. that I am not speaking in generalities or from rumour, but from my own knowledge as a result of information given to me in the penitentiaries as a visitor. Perhaps I have been able to be of some assistance in getting men out on parole, and getting them jobs. And then

I find that time after time they have not been allowed to rehabilitate themselves. I was most interested in one young man who, on release, got a job as a truck driver. Day after day he was stopped on the street when he was recognized, with the result that he was fired. Another man was a recidivist of one of the worst types I have known, and yet toward the end of his last sentence the warden, the padre and the relations officer all said: this man is now reformed. The hon. minister's department let him out on ticket of leave and he got a job. One week later he had that job no longer because the R.C.M.P. went in and told his employer: do you know you have a criminal on your staff, a bank robber? The man got another job, and only 10 days later the same thing happened. He found yet another job, and shortly afterwards he was fired in the same circumstances. Not long ago he came to me and said: "Mr. Winch, I am going to get out of town. I am going to a small village up the coast hoping I will be allowed to redeem myself." I have not seen the man since but I heard about him recently. He was serving three months. Do you know why? It was because he had been stopped again, in this town, by the R.C.M.P. and this time his cup runneth over-he blew his top and socked the cop. He was sentenced to three months for assault.
It goes even beyond that. I have told the committee about this young man who lost job after job because of this hounding practice. He has another brother, a brother who is younger but who looks very like him. That brother has never been in conflict with the law in his life, but because his brother has been in jail four times he is stopped by the police and has lost job after job although he has no criminal record at all. I know this is not done by the majority, but I think that even if this happens only in a minority of cases it is nevertheless of importance. The rehabilitation of men in penitentiaries is, I know, of great concern to the minister, and I have an idea that he is going to bring in some legislation in this field while he is in office.
I am asking the minister whether he does not think that perhaps he might now take the action that was taken four or five years ago when I also raised this matter in the House of Commons and gave instances which were investigated, or at least one case, and as a result the minister's predecessor in office had a directive sent out-and I believe it was sent out by the commissioner-outlining to all officials; not that they all needed it, but some did-that they be very careful not to undermine this process of rehabilitation and establishment of a social consciousness; that if they felt they had to interrogate a person, it should be done on the quiet and not in

public, but under no circumstances were they to go to an employer and have a man fired because he had a previous criminal record.
I just make the suggestion that perhaps the minister might consider the re-issuing of a directive of the nature of the one that was distributed some four or five years ago.
I said, sir, I had two matters relating to the R.C.M.P. These are the matters. I hope the minister will agree with my second proposal but most certainly, sir, not because it affects me, because it does not-I am married; I have three children and five grandchildren; I have done well-but because it affects members of the R.C.M.P. who were born the same way and have the same emotions and feelings as the rest of us. How about relaxing that non-marriage clause and let them build up this country the same as you and I have?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with respect to the two points raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East, I should like to deal with the second one first. The problem of police contacts with persons who are out from penitentiary, having either completed their sentence or are out on parole, is not an easy one because the police recognize as fully as the hon. gentleman does, and as I do, the unfortunate effects of any suggestion of undue supervision or, as he put it, hounding. I can assure him that every effort is made from the top to the bottom to ensure that that will not happen; but, on the other hand, it is still a continuing police duty to check on activities or information coming to their attention which indicate that either investigation or possible action should be taken, and they cannot exempt persons who have been in penitentiary from their normal supervision. It is still part of their duty as police to supervise the conduct of those men to the same extent as it is their obligation to supervise or investigate the conduct of those who may never have been in penitentiary. That is the difficulty with which the force is faced, or with which any police force is faced; but I can assure the hon. gentleman that instructions have been issued-and they are continuing instructions-to which he has referred, to all detachments. I think I had better read the instruction which was issued. It is the one to which the hon. gentleman referred in the committee which sat in the spring of 1957. It reads as follows:
It is sometimes necessary that members of the force inquire into the activities and associates of released convicts or interrogate ex-convicts as to their associations and movements. Such work is a part of police responsibility to the community and nothing in this instruction is to curtail the action of members in the investigation of crime or the proper questioning of suspects.
Inquiries affecting ex-convicts must, however, always be carried out with great care and discretion
Supply-R.C.M.P.
in order that any genuine attempt being made toward rehabilitation will not be hampered or discouraged. Ex-convicts who have resumed or continued a life of crime deserve no special consideration but where there is any indication that a man is making any effort to re-establish himself as a good citizen, any contacts members have with him should be arranged so that his task will not be made more difficult.
The force is vitally interested in rehabilitation work and must always be prepared to assist such efforts in any reasonable manner so long as our actions in that direction do not conflict with our primary police duty of protecting the public and investigating crime.
I am informed that that order or instruction was issued as a permanent instruction to all detachments and that as such it is incorporated in the book of instructions by which all members of the force are bound. We will at all times be prepared, however, to satisfy ourselves that the instruction is properly and sufficiently drawn to the attention of the members of the force. If at any time either from an instance drawn to our attention by others, or from information which we ourselves may bring to light, it should seem that the instruction is not sufficiently widely known or observed, then we shall be prepared to consider issuing some new-not a directive-direction that the instruction be drawn to the attention of all members.
In so far as the instances to which the hon. member refers are concerned, if they are exactly as reported by him, then I would say that if they were carried out by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel in the manner in which the hon. gentleman has outlined, they were contrary to this instruction. But I would suggest to him that he consider carefully first whether in fact in regard to the incident he related, it was a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who was involved. If there is any case that comes to the attention of the hon gentleman or to any other person's attention, in which he has reason to believe that the attitude of the force is not that which they are instructed to observe, if he will bring it to our attention we will be glad to look into the matter.
With regard to the question of marriage, it is a difficult and continuing problem. However, I think the hon. gentleman has overlooked one thing. Probably he is aware of it but forgot to mention it, namely that some two or three years ago the rigid rule regarding five years' service before marriage was relaxed and in certain circumstances members of the force may now marry after three years' service. Therefore, we have made that concession at least-

What happens if he falls in love in the first three years?

Supply-R.C.M.P.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-toward the interest, considerations and requirements to which he has drawn our attention.
I should also point out that the figures of annual wastage from all causes, retirements on pension, discharges and retirements by reason of marriage, are not unduly heavy; indeed, they are satisfactorily light. One always likes to see them as light as possible. In 1957 they amounted to 6.41 per cent for all reasons, as I say, including retirements on pension.
Out of some 2,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite wrong; there are some 5,300 members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Over 300 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will my hon. friend please observe that this is not due to marriage exclusively; this includes wastage for all reasons, the great bulk of which will be retirement on pension, or a very large percentage of which is due to retirement on pension. This is a problem that the authorities are as fully aware of as my hon. friend. The best research and study given to it so far indicates that the purposes and requirements of the force are best served by maintaining a minimum period before marriage is permitted.

Will the minister explain just why it is necessary for the three-year or five-year period? I can assure the Minister of Justice right now that he has in his service a number of young men who are just waiting to hear what he is going to say now so that they may decide whether or not they get out of the force. Why? Because they want to get married. Why should they not be allowed to get married?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As my hon. friend puts it, every man interested in joining the R.C.M.P. is on the verge of marriage but I can assure him that is not the case.
How does the minister know?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are many young men wishing to join the R.C.M.P. who have no present intention of getting married at all and they become recruits. It is pointed out to me that there is a period of one year required for training before the man's recruit training is completed and he can be sent to his first post.
Who knows when love is going to strike?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
His first posting may be to an area where it is just not physically possible or sensible for him to contemplate taking a 
wife. It is for that reason that the requirement of five years or in certain circumstances three years is in the regulations. While, of course, we do not like to think of any potential recruits being barred from the force or in their own judgment finding it not desirable to join because they would rather get married, nevertheless I can assure the hon. gentleman that our recruiting program is going very satisfactorily and that notwithstanding the requirement of abstention from marriage for this limited period we are able to get all the recruits we want within the limitations of the manpower ceiling approved by cabinet.

What happens if after he signs up he meets a girl and falls in love? what are the basic reasons of the R.C.M.P. for having this requirement of five years or three years? Just what does the minister mean by saying that they can get married in three years under certain circumstances? What is behind all this?
Surely not that old shotgun again!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that I mean nothing sinister by that statement nor do I intend any reflection on those who come within the category where marriage after three years is permitted. In certain large communities where we are doing municipal police work and where it is found that the service is not as attractive to single men as service in some of the remote areas, and in certain other circumstances where the duty is not attractive to single men and the circumstances of the duty are such that there is no reason why marriage should not be permitted, then the time limit is reduced to three years. But I am sure the hon. gentleman knows well that there are some areas in which the R.C.M.P. is required to serve and some classes of the duty of that service where marriage is-
Careful now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -admittedly detrimental, shall I say, to the efficient discharge of those duties. We would be accused of being harsh and inhuman if we posted married men to certain areas where the R.C.M.P. have to serve and therefore we have to make the requirement that our recruits do not marry for a minimum period.

Mr. Chairman, there are two matters on which I would appreciate some comment from the minister. One pertains to any change inaugurated by the minister after the famous date of June 10, 1957, which has resulted in substantial savings to the depart-men. Second, I would appreciate some comment from the minister concerning an aspect

of national defence. I raised this question in the estimates committee when we were dealing with North American defence matters and was referred by the chairman of that committee to the minister and his estimates. The matter has to do with defending this continent in ways that are expensive against the arrival of nuclear devices by sea, air or otherwise. I think all members will certainly agree that the Department of National Defence has made a tremendous effort in this regard. However, the possibility does exist of nuclear devices arriving in this country and being planted in a strategic area by a method not already counted by existing defence measures. I refer to the activities of saboteurs and persons of that type. Without wishing any breach of security, I would appreciate some comment from the minister as to what the activities of the mounted police are in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can only answer the second question in a rather general way. We are aware of the potential danger in this regard and that is one of the aspects of the duties of the security and intelligence service of the police, namely so far as possible to identify and keep close track of the movements of potential enemy agents in Canada. In this way we hope to be able to identify any pattern that might develop along the line to which the hon. gentleman refers.
There is also a constant exchange of security information with the security agencies of other friendly countries. In that way we would hope to be informed of any developments or plans to move agents into Canada or any plans that may come to their attention. Further, of course, we are in communication with the armed services of Canada with regard to any information coming to their attention. About all I can say is that we are aware of the potential danger, are taking what steps we can and believe we are taking adequate steps to safeguard against it.
With regard to the matter of savings initiated since we took office in June of 1957, we have reviewed the purchase policy in all fields but particularly with respect to automobiles and also our policy with regard to the use and life of automobiles. While I am unable to give my hon. friend any particulars because the factors here are difficult to isolate with particularity, we believe we have been able to effect substantial savings as a result of the new policy.

Many thousands of visitors to Canada travel hundreds of miles for the one express purpose of seeing our Royal Canadian Mounted Police, only to return to their countries sadly disappointed because they did
Supply-R.C.M.P.
not have the privilege even of catching a glimpse of what they recognize is the finest and most colourful body of men in the world. Perhaps this is one of the reasons why these young men are the object of special attention by so many young ladies who are not slow in laying siege to capture them. Here we have a situation not so much of a force that gets its man but of the dear ladies capturing members of the force.
Pictures of mounties are found on postcards, souvenirs and government advertising folders and literature urging visitors to come to Canada. No wonder they are disappointed when they do not see these men. We in Canada should feel proud that our country has become favoured because of many reasons, not the least of which is the fact that we can point with pride to the finest group of men in the world upholding law and order in the land.
It seems to me, therefore, that all should see to it that there are enough of them so that every visitor will be able to return home with the satisfaction that his trip to Canada was made more enjoyable and exciting because he actually saw a Royal Canadian Mounted policeman. We are anxious to relieve unemployment. What more beneficial method could we adopt than to build up the strength of our mounted police force to a point where we would be assured of having one or two mounted police officers at each point of entry into Canada. I am only asking the minister if he will tell the house whether or not an increase in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is contemplated? I trust the minister will give this some consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am very glad to assure the hon. gentleman that we are giving constant consideration to this problem because it is one of the real problems which which we are faced, not so much in the discharge of the duties of a working police force as in what I might call the incidental fields. This is a real and continuing problem. One of the things which give me and all the members of the force, from the commissioner down, very real satisfaction is that people want to see the full uniform, that is the red coat of the mounted police, because it does typify in the public mind the character and reputation of that force. But my hon. friend appreciates that it is not possible to discharge the real day-to-day work of a police force in that uniform. Our first essential is to do the job of a police force. If we do not do that, then it would not matter how splendidly the force was dressed or how colourful the uniform, the reputation would not be there. Every

Supply-R.C.M.P.
officer and man of the force also appreciates that. Our problem, therefore, is to reconcile the necessity of carrying on the ordinary everyday duties of a police force, and yet accept the numerous requests that come in, such as the one made by the hon. gentleman, that we should have a man in full dress uniform at border crossing points.
Every time we accept one request we find it lands us in greater difficulty because someone else will say, you have done it for them so now you have to do it for us. We have had to restrict, therefore, to a minimum the number of occasions and areas in which we provide a man in a scarlet uniform, tunic and breeches, for what I might call display or parade purposes. I do not decry, for a moment, parade and display when properly used, but we have to keep it under control. It is only at such points as Ottawa, certain provincial capitals and one or two other places, where we make this concession to the desire of Canadians and tourists to see mounted police constables in bright uniforms.
However, as I have said, we are giving consideration to meeting these requests, and wherever a request for a special appearance appears a reasonable one we do our best to comply with it. We have a problem right now with regard to the strength of the force. We are by no means overmanned. Indeed, I believe if there is anything in that way it lies in the other direction. We are unable, therefore, to comply with the suggestion the hon. member makes. It could be that one day when we are fully manned and feel we have reached a strength where every duty can be complied with and still leave some men over for the type of appearance that the hon. gentleman has in mind, then we would be glad indeed to supply the largest number of men we could under the circumstances to which he has referred.

I do not want to take up too much time of the committee but there are

a few observations I should like to put on the record. They have to do with the administration of justice in general in this country and especially with the appointment of judges of the superior courts as they are called, in the province of Quebec or judges of the supreme court of the other provinces and also the judges of the court of Queen's Bench.
There are a number of systems, as I know, with regard to the appointment of judges around the world. In some countries students, when they take law, decide that they want to become judges. They therefore direct their studies especially to that end and the government of the country-and I think this is especially true for France-appoints those students as judges when they have completed their studies. I do not think this system should be applied to Canada. I think that the system as it is now in this country is sound and good. It is true that the criticism is sometimes made that the government of this country-whether the former government or this one-appoints political partisans to the bench. I have no objection to that procedure, and I am not saying that because I am a lawyer and may be aspiring to an appointment to the bench; I am quite sure that I will not be appointed during the next four years. However, it is true that the government appoint lawyers to the bench, especially lawyers who have had a very active practice and at the same time a very active political career. In my opinion it is a good thing that this is so. There is no other field in which one can learn so much of human nature as can be learned by engaging in politics. This is the place where we meet more people and where we can learn more of the human character. It is also true that those lawyers who have extensive practices are better qualified to be good judges.
There is a particular problem that affects the citizens of this country in general and also, of course, the citizens of Quebec. I do not agree with the statement of the premier of Quebec that here in Ottawa we are elsewhere. I think we are in our own country whether we are in Ottawa, in Quebec or anywhere else in the country. I make this suggestion to the minister and in doing so may I say that I appreciate the fact that the matter is not entirely in the field of jurisdiction of this government. The federal government do not establish the number of judges in the provinces. That is true especially, I am sure, for the province of Quebec; it is a matter which appertains to the premier of Quebec. I refer to the determination of the number of judges of the superior court.

I know that not enough judges are appointed in the province of Quebec and I also know that not enough are appointed in some other provinces either. I know that, Mr. Chairman, because your father is the chief justice of the province of Quebec and he is complaining every year that the number of judges is not commensurate with the number of cases to be heard.
In my own district which was established in 1956 there are over 100 cases on the list and not one that has been inscribed there since July 1, 1956 has been heard. As far as I know this situation prevails all over. It is not right that the citizens of Canada who want to put their cases before the court should be confronted with the situation that it takes a year, a year and a half, two years, or maybe three years to be heard. The witnesses may no longer be there. Sometimes they are dead. They may have moved out of the district. It is extremely hard for our clients to come before the courts three years and maybe four years after an accident has taken place; I am referring to automobile accident cases especially. I suggest that some step should be taken, either by correspondence or otherwise with the provincial authorities, to appoint more judges.
I should like to make another suggestion, namely that more consideration be given to the appointment as judges of lawyers who are practising in the country rather than in the cities. I congratulate the Minister of Justice because I know he appointed in the province of Quebec at least two or four who where lawyers practising in small cities and in the country. I have nothing against lawyers practising in big cities but they are more or less becoming specialists in some cases whereas those who are practising in the country-and the minister knows this- are obliged to carry on a wider practice.
Those were the few remarks I wished to make. I am sure that in the future, as has been the case in the past, the Minister of Justice who has the responsibility of recommending the appointments, will appoint judges who will discharge their duties in the best way possible and always with great honesty.

Mr. Chairman, before considering the estimates of the Department of Justice in detail, may I be allowed to make a few remarks of a general nature, which I consider germane to the debate just begun. As I do not wish to obstruct the business of the house, I shall try to be clear, brief and accurate.
