First of all, I want to tell the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) how happy we have been to learn these last few days, that he had entrusted some lawyers with the study of a report published last spring by the commission on restrictive trade practices, with regard to the purchase of pulpwood from our farmers, and, if there is ground, to take legal action as provided by statute. Having been among the first, during this session, to stress the importance of the matter and the urgent need of government action, I now ought to tender my most sincere congratulations to the hon. minister. His attitude, which is that of the government, eloquently proves that, in this country, there is only one law for all citizens, that before the law nobody is too great or too small, nor too powerful or too weak, and that anybody who does not observe it can incur punitive action, which the courts are authorized to impose.
Moroever, during the last few days, the hon. minister informed this house that in September, he would invite the attorney generals of all the provinces to Ottawa to discuss with them the report of the Fauteux commission and to determine any legislation which should follow upon that report. As everyone knows, some findings of the report call for various changes in the way justice is now administered by the provinces. Rather than take the initiative of legislating alone, the Conservative government has chosen to consult the provinces so as to base its action on their views in this matter, if necessary. This action contrasts with certain unilateral practices of which the former government was so fond. It shows the concern for the constitution, which now obtains, as well as the concern for the constitutional powers of the provinces. It is such as to create an atmosphere of mutual confidence and contribute efficiently to the maintenance of national unity. The Minister of Justice and the government of the country deserve congratulations and thanks on that score.
This Fauteux report has reference to social and legal problems in which anybody who has anything to do with social services or the administration of justice must take an active interest. Among those who, in the district of Quebec, have always been interested in this, there was Hon. Justice Oscar Boulanger, who died suddenly a few days ago and whose memory it is appropriate to recall here. He sat in this house as member for Bellechasse from 1926 to 1940 and had a particularly active and fruitful parliamentary life. He has left the memory of a parliamentarian imbued with the purest patriotism, a patriotism rooted in the soil of the constituency of Bellechasse where he was born and where the land has remained the great provider not only on a

strictly material basis but even more so on the moral and intellectual level.
In 1940, he abandoned politics for the bench. Having had many an occasion to plead before him, I came to appreciate his legal knowledge, his acute sense of justice, and his perfect integrity. He rose all the more in the estimation of litigants because his conscience dictated an equitable approach to the sometimes overstringent requirements of the law. It was through this balanced formula that he sought justice, and strove to assure it of victory.
He had two other betes noires: perjury, and misuse of French. The newspaper L'Action Catholique, in its issue of 22nd July last, recalled this aspect of his temperament as follows:
Though not a purist, he readily took up the cudgels, on behalf of the French language, against habitual users of incorrect terms and anglicisms, especially in cases having to do with automobile accidents. He would indignantly flay, sometimes with bitter irony, witnesses oblivious of the solemnity of their oath, bent on toying with the truth.
The career of Hon. Justice Boulanger once again leads to the conclusion that, in principle, there is no reason why magistrates should not, at times, be selected among lawyers who have been in politics. To his legal training, to his experience as a practitioner, to the integrity which is the first requirement to his admission to and maintenance in the bar association, the parliamentary lawyer generally adds a degree of psychology, of knowledge and of broadmindedness which can be acquired only here and which will be of great assistance to him in untangling the tragedies of which court proceedings are but the outcome.
In a speech made in 1853, protesting against the suggestion that the Master of the Rolls be ineligible to the House of Commons, Lord Macaulay said:
(Text):
I believe that there is a close connection between the functions of the law-givers as between anatomy and surgery. Would it not be the height of absurdity to lay down the rule that nobody who dissected the dead should be allowed to operate on the living?
(Translation):
Et plus loin:
(Text):
Who can be so well qualified to make laws and to mend laws as a man whose business is to interpret laws and to administer laws?
(Translation):
Without going as far as Lord Macaulay, and without holding the view that it would still be appropriate for a man to be at one and the same time a judge and a legislator, the fact

remains that this reasoning could then be justified by experience going back several centuries.
Far be it from me to suggest that magistrates should invariably be chosen from among lawyers who have been in politics! All I am trying to emphasize is that there is no objection in principle. In a remarkable work, The Machinery of Justice in England, Professor R. M. Jackson hits the nail on the head when he states:
(Text):
There has been no apparent connection in the last hundred years between the political antecedents of judges and the decisions of those judges. The point is primarily one of public confidence, that people may feel sure that those on the bench have been appointed for legal eminence and suitability and not for political reward or by way of disposing of an embarrassing political colleague.
(Translation):
Regardless of whether he has a political background, the magistrate of our time and place surely receives great help from his guarantees and privileges: he is shielded from governmental influences by his irremovability; he is protected from the snare of his own ambition by lack of promotion; and he is guarded from abuse of duty by his fixed salary and widow's pension. It was Sir Robert Walpole, that great leader of men, who defined gratitude as "the hope of new favours''; and he added that men "are less concerned with what they've got than with what they're going to get". That is just it; once a judge has been appointed, he has no further goal to reach out for. There is only one final reward which he seeks and which he can hope for, and that is the satisfaction of having done his duty-thus participating in that nobly social work that is the administration of justice.
Such, Mr. Chairman, were the thoughts that came to my mind when I reflected on the premature demise of the Hon. Justice Oscar Boulanger. My heartfelt sympathy goes out to his family, to his former electors in Belle-chasse, and to those in this house who knew him and shared my feelings for him. Let there be no doubt that he will forever remain, for us, a shining beacon of example and inspiration.

the way of guesswork and surmise that I believe we would all appreciate any information the minister feels he can give us at this time on the narcotics situation in this country, in particular any views he may have as to the treatment of addicts.
I believe we all recognize the seriousness of the situation and I understand from the reports of the commission on narcotic drugs in the United Nations that it is estimated there are somewhere in the neighbourhood of 5,000 addicts in Canada, of whom it is estimated over half are on the Pacific coast.
I believe we all recognize not only the seriousness of the narcotic addiction situation itself but the enormous cost that is involved, the millions of dollars spent on the illicit trade and also the millions of dollars involved because of the need of the addicts to get money in order to buy their supplies, to obtain which they resort, in most cases, to crime. I have always been somewhat intrigued in reading the journals of the commission of the United Nations on narcotic drugs to note how in so many countries they do not have the same type or degree of narcotic situation as we have here in Canada. I have one of those reports before me now, and it is interesting to note that in the United Kingdom, where I believe they have a population of some 45 million, they have a record of only 335 addicts, and all those addicts, so the report states, are receiving their drugs from licit sources by licit means.
This should give us some reason to pause and think. I will not say that I believe I know the answer. I know that a study of this situation was made by a committee of the other house a couple of years ago which brought down a comprehensive report. That committee had its views on the subject, but I am not going to say I agree with those views. I know that we have what is called the English system, and some people believe in it and others do not, including one high authority in British Columbia. I know, also, that something else was tried in the United States which has been approved by some and discounted by others. I am not going to put myself up as any kind of authority, but I have been interested in this problem, as was my late father, for many years, and there must be an answer somewhere.
At least we should be trying something new. Surely, we cannot continue any longer with the situation which exists at the present time. On one issue I am very definite. As far as the pusher is concerned, I believe he should be treated with all the severity of the law. By "pusher" I mean the pedlar, the man who makes a profit out of the narcotic hunger of the addict. I have no hesitation in saying that as far as these people are concerned I

Supply-Justice
would go even further than the present law prescribes as to penalties.
Capital punishment?

No, you are not going to catch me on that. I will go right up to life imprisonment. I also feel strongly that we would have some semblance of control if we could take the profit motive out of the illicit trade, and the only way to do that would be to recognize that addiction is an illness, and treat it as such. I have been interested in reading about the methods used in the majority of the countries of the world. In most cases, I find there is no compulsory registration of addicts nor is there compulsory notification of addiction. There is not even compulsory treatment of addiction. I find this rather strange, and I do think that perhaps we should give serious thought to requiring the compulsory notification of addicts, and registration of addiction so that there may be a record and so that cases of addiction can be followed up in order to try to persuade these people to take proper treatment and become rehabilitated. I do not see how this can be done unless there is some system of registration.
I am not going to say that there should be free drugs, because I admit I am a little afraid of the principle of free drugs, but I do say there might well be free treatment of addicts and this would mean the establishment of addiction treatment centres. As I said before, I have nothing conclusive in mind, nor is my mind set in any distinct channel as to how to make the best approach to this most serious problem in our country, but in view of the fact that I have read so many articles in the press of recent weeks commenting on the subject or trying to guess what is in the mind of the minister, I feel that he must have some thoughts on the problem at this stage and that even if he has not yet decided on any final policy he might now be in a position to give some interim information to the committee and make some recommendations as to how we might deal with this difficult problem.

I appreciate very much the words of the hon. member for Vancouver East. I know of his concern with this problem of narcotics and of the contribution and study that he has made to it. I wish that I could comply with his request for a definite statement. I will be as definite as I can but I am unable to be as definite as I would like to be as to our policy.
I can tell him, however, that the studies are progressing. We are not letting the matter drop, nor are we slackening in our intent or our desire to arrive at a solution, at least at a solution in our minds which we can present to parliament. I think with him that it is going to be very difficult for anyone to say that he has the complete answer even after he studies it. We must arrive at a decision, yes, but even then we would not want to be dogmatic about it. But we agree, I think, that we have to try something different when

the present system is not working. Studies are proceeding on an informal committee basis between my own departmental officials, the R.C.M.P. and the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I hope, at any rate,-and I do not think it is too much to say-that we may be able to present a series of amendments or proposals to amend the Criminal Code next year. I hope it is not too much to say that we shall be able to present a proposal with regard to narcotics. At the same time, I would like to make one thing clear with regard to suggestions that I myself have made from time to time as to one possible solution of this problem.
I want to emphasize, first, that I have never gone beyond saying that this is one possible solution that we should look at. I have never said that this is the only solution, but I have referred to a possibility of establishing clinics for the treatment of convicted addicts. To judge by newspaper comments, some have taken from my remarks the idea that I was suggesting that we should establish institutions for the free distribution of drugs. This is the furthest thing from my thoughts. I think it would be a retrograde step. The idea of a convicted addict coming in and getting drugs handed to him to be taken by him, or taken away and used by him, without supervision, I never had in mind. I am quite sure that, as far as we can go, if a solution along this line is to be adopted, is to establish clinics.
There, as part of the condition upon which he may be released from penitentiary, the convicted addict might come in and be administered the minimum required dose under the supervision of a properly established and staffed medical clinic.
That, I think, would go a long way, if it is found to be feasible, toward this objective which the hon. gentleman and I, and I think everybody, have in mind. That is, taking the profit out of the drug traffic and also putting on a scientific and social basis our attitude toward addicts who, as the hon. gentleman says, are-while they may have committed crimes to obtain drugs and nearly all addicts have been guilty of crime-unfortunately ill. They are not only criminals, they are also ill.
But I think I must say to him that it would not be possible, as I see it, for this parliament to go beyond setting up those clinics for the treatment of convicted addicts. We could have no jurisdiction whatsoever to set up clinics to which persons who are self-confessed addicts might come. That would require action on the part of the provincial governments, or possibly some joint action between the dominion and the provinces. We ourselves have no jurisdiction to take power to treat

the warden was to be present. The man's legal counsel was not to be present nor was permission given for any written statement of the charges which resulted in the ticket of leave being rescinded. Nobody but the remission service agent and Mr. Munavish knows what went on between them and we have to take the word of the one or the other.
Since that time I have received from the counsel for Mr. Munavish an affidavit made and sworn to by Mr. Munavish in which he denies all the allegations as they were given to him by the agent of the remissions branch when he met Mr. Munavish at the B.C. penitentiary on instructions of the Minister of Justice. Under circumstances of that nature what do we do? The Minister of Justice will admit that the only thing I could do when I received the affidavit from the man in the penitentiary and advice from his counsel was to raise the matter as I am now doing as an example of the principle of a man not having a right to a trial, shall I say, a right to be heard in his own defence when his ticket of leave is cancelled and he is returned to what could be, although we hope not, a life term in a penitentiary of this country.
To me there is something wrong. I know the view of the Minister of Justice and I want to thank him publicly for having invited me to his office, spending considerable time discussing this case and giving me information which I am not allowed to disclose because I was taken into the confidence of the minister. But having all that in mind, to me there is something wrong when a man, having been released on the authority of the remission service, has his ticket of leave cancelled without reasons being given, without an opportunity to defend himself, particularly when by affidavit he denies every charge made against him, and there is no procedure whatsoever that I know of unless the minister will use-is it sections 14 and 15?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, again I appreciate the hon. gentleman's interest in this case and the point of view from which he approaches it. It is a point of view with which I have every sympathy but I think I can say, and I hope I will be able to convince him, that it is a point of view that is not applicable to cases of parole or ticket of leave as it is now called. It is not applicable because what the hon. gentleman is asking for is a formal charge and a formal trial. He said that if the man is convicted he might be sentenced to penitentiary for a further period of years and then everybody will know and it will be justified.
But the reason I say that the principle of the right to a trial enunciated by the hon. member is not applicable here is that the man is not charged with any offence. He is not charged with an offense for which he can be tried. What has happened is that the parole authority, in the conscientious discharge of the duties of its position of supervising this man who was out on ticket of leave, has reported that in its opinion the circumstances are such that the interests of society, and in this case I can also say the interests of the man, require his recommittal to penitentiary. It is not that an offence had been committed but that it felt, and the knowledge in its possession was such, that if the man were left at large another offence would be committed.
Remember that parolees-I will call them that although, strictly speaking, they are not to be called that until the new bill goes through-are not persons whose sentences have been commuted. They have not been made the subjects of diminution of their sentences by exercise of an act of clemency. Their sentences are still in existence. Suppose their sentence is 12 years and they are paroled at the end of 6 or 7 years. The sentence is not commuted but still has 5 or 6 years to run, as the case may be. It is simply that it is found that they are able to serve the balance of their sentences outside the penitentiary on condition that they submit to the supervision of a parole officer and report from time to time with varying degrees of frequency.
It is a licence. It is not a shortening of the sentence. The sentence is still there and
Supply-Justice
all that happens is that if the parole authority has reason to believe that the interests of society or the welfare of the man demand it, it so reports and the man may then be recommitted to the institution for the purpose of investigation, first of all as to whether in fact his parole should be suspended or revoked.
In this case, an investigation has taken place, and for the time being this parole has been revoked. This does not mean that the man may not be released on parole again.
There is, I know, more to say about this, Mr. Chairman, but what I have tried to do is state the broad principles upon which parole proceeds. I see it is now 4.30.

Water Resources-Proposed Chicago Diversion

subtopic: CHICAGO DIVERSION

speechtext:
Useful conversations between United States and Canadian officials were held in Ottawa on July 7, 1957 on the subject of the sanitation problems which gave rise to proposed legislation for a three-year temporary diversion of 1,000 cubic feet of water per second from the great lakes system and on the subject of studies to be carried out under the proposed legislation.
The Canadian government understands that if such legislation is enacted these sanitation studies will not be limited to evaluating the effects of dilution but will also include consideration of all possible measures for dealing with waste disposal facilities at Chicago. Such measures would include:
(a)	complete separation of storm sewers from the domestic sewerage system or expansion of the existing treatment facilities to serve a total combined flow;
(b)	treatment of organic wastes in industrial plants before discharging these effluents into the sewerage system;
(c)	chlorination of effluent before discharge into the Illinois waterway; and
(d)	artificial aeration of the waterway.
The treatment of sewage in the Chicago
area is, of course, a matter entirely within the jurisdiction of the competent legislative bodies within the United States. It is understood that present treatment of waste represents a vast improvement over conditions which existed in former years and that
under the present day uses of the water the waste is more a nuisance than a menace to the public health in the area.
In considering the economics of alternative methods of improved waste disposal, it is assumed that full consideration will be given to the economic harm which may be done to navigation and hydro-electric generation in both countries by extended use of dilution methods.
It is not possible to give a firm undertaking to provide flows of a particular volume through the existing Long Lac and Ogoki diversions to the great lakes basin during the three-year period envisaged by proposed United States legislation. However, if it were possible to offset part of the effects of the Chicago diversion by inflows from the Albany basin in Canada, it would be equitable that an equivalent amount of water should remain available for use in hydroelectric power generation by the Ontario interests at St. Marys falls, Niagara falls and in the international section of the St. Lawrence river until the effects of the proposed temporary diversion will have ceased to be felt in the great lakes system.
All rights under the provisions of the boundary waters treaty of 1909 are specifically reserved.
The Canadian Embassy
Washington,
January 6, 1958.
